title: How to See Your Work as Worship
excerpt: Work is not a punishment God invented after the fall. It was there in the garden first. Here is how to recover that, on a Monday, in a job you did not choose.
body:
Most of us learned that work is a curse and Sunday is the reward. The week is what you survive so you can get to the part where God shows up. This is exactly backwards, and it has quietly ruined a lot of lives, including some of mine.

Go back to the beginning. Before there is sin, before there is a single broken thing in the world, there is work. Genesis puts Adam in the garden "to work it and keep it." The word translated *work* there is the same word used elsewhere for serving God, for worship. Work and worship were not two activities. They were one. The fall did not invent labor. It made labor painful, frustrating, full of thorns. But it did not change what work is for.

So when we treat our jobs as the godless part of the week, we are not being humble. We are repeating the fall's lie that the ordinary world is no place to meet God.

## Stop dividing the sacred from the secular

The first move is to kill the line you have drawn down the middle of your life. On one side: prayer, church, your Bible. On the other: spreadsheets, drywall, the third meeting that should have been an email. You have decided one side is God's and the other side is just yours.

There is no such line in Scripture. Paul tells slaves, people in the least dignified work imaginable, to do their labor "as for the Lord and not for men." If a first-century slave could turn his work into worship, your job is not disqualified by being boring or underpaid.

This week, name the place where you have drawn that line most sharply. For me it was email. I had decided email was beneath God's attention, which meant I did it carelessly, resentfully, late. The work did not change. My account of it had to.

## Ask what your work serves

Work is worship when it serves your neighbor. That is the bridge. Luther called ordinary jobs "masks of God," the means by which God feeds and clothes and protects people without showing his face. The farmer is how God feeds the city. The nurse is how God's care reaches a body in pain. The accountant is how a family does not lose its house.

So ask of your actual job: who is fed, healed, housed, taught, protected because I did this well today? If you cannot find anyone, that is worth sitting with. Sometimes it means the work is genuinely empty and you should leave it. More often it means you have stopped looking at the human being on the other end of what you make.

## Do the work well, not just visibly

Worship is not done for an audience. Neither is faithful work. The temptation at every job is to optimize for what is seen, to perform diligence when the boss walks by and coast when he does not.

The craftsman who tightens the joint no inspector will ever check is closer to worship than the loud Christian who quotes verses at the water cooler and ships sloppy work. God sees the joint. That is the whole point of "as for the Lord." The audience is not your manager. It is the One who counts the hairs on your head.

I have shipped sloppy work and told myself it didn't matter because nobody would know. Somebody knew. I knew. And the God I claim to worship was standing in the room while I cut the corner.

## Let the frustration preach to you

Here is the part the cheerful version of this leaves out. Your work is still under the curse. There are still thorns. The project will fail, the customer will be cruel, the effort will go unrewarded. Treating work as worship does not make it stop hurting.

But the frustration itself can become honest prayer. When the thing breaks for the fourth time, you are feeling, in your body, the gap between the world God made and the world as it is. That ache is not faithlessness. It is the groaning Paul says the whole creation is doing, waiting to be set right. You are allowed to bring that to God instead of pretending the office is fine.

Work as worship is not work without grief. It is grief offered up instead of swallowed.

## This week

Pick one task you usually do with resentment or on autopilot. Before you start it, say one sentence out loud: *I am doing this for you, and for whoever it serves.* Then do it as if God were the only one watching, because in the only account that finally matters, he is. Notice what changes in the doing. Notice, too, what does not, and bring that to him as well.

You will not feel transfigured. The spreadsheet will still be a spreadsheet. But you will have begun to close the wound the fall opened, the lie that God is somewhere other than the middle of your ordinary week.
